Apple adds new disk controls to prevent AI agents from running amok

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (418 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mac consumers will be warned of the risks of granting AI full disk access.
  • Sources indicate that after sounding an alarm about the glitch last month, Apple is taking steps to limit Mac disk access to AI agents, the tech giant declared on its developer blog.
  • The concern rose to prominence in September, when Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mac consumers will be warned of the risks of granting AI full disk access.

Sources indicate that after sounding an alarm about the glitch last month, Apple is taking steps to limit Mac disk access to AI agents, the tech giant declared on its developer blog. In its latest macOS beta, Apple introduced controls to ensure that customers will need to take "very explicit" actions to grant apps like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini "this extraordinary level of [full disk] access.".

The concern rose to prominence in September, when Inc. columnist Jason Aten noticed that Meta's Muse Mac app was able to access his messages even though he thought he had denied that permission. Meta argued that Aten must have granted access, saying the feature is entirely opt-in, but the incident caught Apple's eye. "Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems — including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history — without users' full knowledge and understanding," Apple wrote.

It has been revealed that apple vowed to address the concern with upcoming disk controls. As screen grabs from X user @madeby_ldt show, Apple's Full Disk Access setting now requires explicit permissions to be granted from a scary-looking pop-up screen. It states, "Your Mac will not be able to protect your data from [your desired AI app]," and forces you to review and OK the actions it will be able to take. Those include "Read, Change, Delete and Export all your Data," "View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos," and "View History and Browser as You.".

Industry observers note that the upcoming controls won't stop owners from granting AI agents access to your files, but it should give them pause. If one of those AI agents goes rogue — which is something we've seen before — they could potentially leak or misuse your private data. Stopping this is key for Mac models like the Studio that Apple is specifically marketing for local AI models and agents.

According to recent reports, "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring people clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy," Apple mentioned last month. The newly introduced feature is now out on macOS 27.3 beta 2, but there's no word on when it will be released to all users.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, disney is also expanding vertical videos on Disney Plus, which it first brought to the app in March.

A unified Disney Plus and Hulu app has been a long time coming. Disney started testing its “one-app experience” in 2023, which involved putting a Hulu app tile in the Disney Plus app. This initial experience didn’t include all of Hulu’s content, though, including certain demonstrates, live TV channels, and premium add-ons. This upcoming merger will change this by folding all of Hulu into Disney Plus, creating “a seamless way to discover and engage” with content across both services, according to Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston. Disney still hasn’t confirmed whether it will shut down the standalone Hulu app.

According to recent reports, disney is also expanding vertical videos on Disney Plus, which it first brought to the app in March. The firm looks to introduce videos from TikTok creators in December, as well as add more live sports and podcasts to the service.

Breaking: Nvidia’s first massive move after Jensen Huang’s exit targets national security

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.
  • Nvidia said Tuesday that the fresh standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks.
  • According to recent reports, the Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce upcoming export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.

Nvidia said Tuesday that the fresh standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.

According to recent reports, the Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce upcoming export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.

The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the tech giant to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Collette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.

In a recent development, the committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.

Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.

Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month.

Breaking: Fed’s Kevin Warsh indicates AI empowers bad actors as staff model AI scenarios

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at the FOMC press conference in Washington on 16 September 2026.
  • Federal Reserve staff have started drawing up scenarios for how AI could play out in the US economy, chairman Kevin Warsh said on Monday.
  • Industry observers note that “SI empowers all, including bad actors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at the FOMC press conference in Washington on 16 September 2026.

Federal Reserve staff have started drawing up scenarios for how AI could play out in the US economy, chairman Kevin Warsh said on Monday. They range from a broad growth boom to a downturn if the technology disappoints. He also told a Fed conference in San Francisco that AI gives upcoming power to bad actors.

Industry observers note that “SI empowers all, including bad actors. So, we’re thinking especially of critical infrastructures and their vulnerabilities,” Warsh stated.

Sources indicate that warsh opened the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted with the San Francisco Fed and livestreamed. He used “SI”, for super intelligence, throughout, the term the US government adopted after Trump’s executive order. The Fed has published his prepared remarks.

Industry observers note that the Board’s staff is using stylised, model-based frameworks to generate scenarios, Warsh noted. He called them illustrative, not forecasts or predictions.

In the first, AI raises productivity and the gains are shared between workers and the owners of capital. Real GDP grows above its long-run average and the US stays close to full employment.

In the second, growth still rises above average, but AI displaces jobs rather than complementing them. Automation and frictions in the labour market push unemployment above full-employment levels.

In the third, AI disappoints. After heavy investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and valuations could fall, leading to a slowdown and a rise in unemployment. The economy would recover, he mentioned, but without the productivity gains.

“Humans are the designers and the builders, and humans must be the deciders,” Warsh remarked.

Industry observers note that he did not comment on interest rates. He also did not address AI’s effect on inflation, as the Associated Press noted, though several Fed officials have tied the data centre buildout to rising prices.

Industry observers note that warsh then moderated a panel with Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison and Affirm CEO Max Levchin. Asked how worried people should be about cybersecurity, Arora remarked AI can now find flaws in code written over the past 50 years.

In a recent development, “It’s not that the hackers have become smarter. The technology has become so good even bad hackers have become okay,” Arora noted.

In a recent development, arora mentioned Mythos, which came out six months ago, is now within reach of most bad actors through open-source models. Outside security help is booked up, he said, because every company is fending off attempts to get into its systems. He called the next two to three years a “technology rebuild moment”.

Collison agreed. Even the Linux TCP stack, one of the most scrutinised pieces of software, turned out to be full of exploitable bugs, he said. Levchin called the attackers’ edge a temporary effect that would end in sturdier software.

It has been revealed that on jobs, Levchin said Affirm’s engineers are about five times more productive, with “zero layoffs due to AI”. Collison said Stripe is hiring far less for general and administrative roles but more engineers and salespeople. New businesses launching on Stripe each week are up about twofold year on year, he said.

US stocks extended an AI sell-off on Monday. The Nasdaq 100 dropped nearly 3%, and selling picked up in the afternoon as investors took in Warsh’s comments, Business Insider reported. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, and Anthropic is due to price its IPO on Wednesday.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, TRMNL, the tech giant known for e-paper frames and kits, just debuted its biggest and most colorful product yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s mounted in a handmade wooden frame and will be released in limited numbers.

According to recent reports, TRMNL, the tech giant known for e-paper frames and kits, just debuted its biggest and most colorful product yet. Frame is a 31.5-inch full color e-paper display mounted in a handmade wooden frame, designed to show paintings, photos, maps, graphics and other still images in a more natural way than LCD or OLED screens. Though not cheap, it features high-quality materials and will be released in limited numbers to start with.

Recent findings suggest that if you've never heard of TRMNL, the tech giant has had some buzz of late with its e-paper displays sold in frames or kits. Thus far, products like the DIY (kit) and OG (picture frame) have been strictly black and white or grayscale, because "TRMNL is not a television. We avoid trying to do too much," founder Ryan Kulp explained in a blog post.

According to recent reports, however, the introduction of grayscale with the OG model apparently got the company thinking that color "aligns with our vision and just maybe, it makes it even better," Kulp wrote. To that end, TRMNL introduced the full-color e-paper Frame, set to ship by late 2026 or early 2027 for $1,300 in a first batch of around 470 units.

"Over the past few months we've been developing Lazarus, a color conversion engine that we think provides Frame the best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display," Kulp wrote. "And yes it will be open source for your own tuning pleasure.".

To further improve picture quality, Frame will use clock sync to reduce flicker and extend battery life. Though internet connected, it offers a microSD port if you prefer to run it offline. Along with a rechargeable battery, you get a rear USB-C port with a small hole through the back panel for always-on connectivity. It can be hung in portrait or landscape orientation, and you can optionally buy or build your own kickstand.

Sources indicate that TRMNL is working on community developers on other features and even "created a Local Art plugin where anyone can submit their work and even sell it through the TRMNL platform." The organization promises a transparent supply chain and has everything it needs to build Frame "in stock or on order" for a smooth fulfillment cycle. Everything is assembled by its team and not outsourced.

Sources indicate that pre-orders are now open starting at $1,300, with the first batch shipping to the USA, Canada, Mexico and Australia. Potential buyers outside those countries can still get in on the action by pre-ordering here, though the TRMNL said that "duty/import fees could be quite high given the product's customs value." Next year, it plans to open another woodworking shop near its Berlin warehouse to offer "postage- and duty-free fulfillment.".

#920. Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1636 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you?
  • Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell.
  • Industry observers note that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you? To leave you emotionally battered, physically exhausted, and full of despair and hope at the same time? Then allow me to prescribe a healthy dose of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film in the Hunger Games series.

Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. These are the biggest Hunger Games yet, with 48 tributes instead of the standard 24. Among them is Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor to series protagonists Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

Industry observers note that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games. We know, by virtue of the entire original trilogy, that he does. But before he was the cynical, heavy-drinking, lone wolf victor audiences met in The Hunger Games, he was an optimistic 16-year-old with a caring family, a loving relationship, and a solid community in District 12. So the real question of Sunrise on the Reaping becomes, what broke that young man down so thoroughly? The answer is, unsurprisingly, bleak as all hell. But director Francis Lawrence executes it in thrilling (if occasionally overstuffed) fashion, with a Hunger Games sequence that blows series-high Catching Fire's own games out of the water, and a dogged focus on the philosophical themes at the core of Collins' work.

This being a Hunger Games movie, there are certain key beats it needs to hit. First, tributes need to be reaped. In this case, District 12's motley crew is made up of Haymitch, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). From there, the tributes must go to the Capitol and witness its gaudy depravity for themselves. They get makeovers, train, give interviews, and eventually make their way into the Capitol's ultimate death trap.

In a recent development, viewers have seen these beats before in The Hunger Games and Catching Fire. They also witnessed a deliberately scaled-back version in prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which established the Games' evolution from what was essentially a run-down cage match to a glossy propaganda spectacle.

According to recent reports, after sending us through three very different Hunger Games, how can the franchise create a new variation on the same brutal theme? First, by making Sunrise on the Reaping a heist movie. Granted, Haymitch and his allies aren't actually trying to steal anything from the Capitol. Rather, they're trying to break the arena and send a clear message. For that, Haymitch gets roped into a scheme cooked up by former victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and his son, District 3 tribute Ampert (Percy Daggs IV). With a complex series of moving parts, Ampert and Haymitch's plan captures the essence of a dangerous heist, and Lawrence delivers the suspense to match.

Then, there's the arena. If you thought Catching Fire's clock was a sadistic marvel of game-making, not to mention a visual feast thanks to its tropical jungles and beaches, get ready for a level up. The arena for the Second Quarter Quell is a technicolor nightmare. Lush flower beds and crystal clear streams hide poisonous underbellies. Swarms of beautiful birds and butterflies will kill at a moment's notice. Even an idyllic, snow-capped mountain hides explosive horrors. Thankfully, Sunrise on the Reaping is actually colorful to match, its eye-popping hues reminding blockbuster filmmakers everywhere that yes, vibrancy is still possible!

Sources indicate that that vibrancy in Sunrise on the Reaping extends to the broader world of Panem itself, which has taken on a distinctive '70s look. The Capitol is awash in glitzy psychedelics, a far cry from the post-war dilapidation of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. As the Games have grown more extravagant, so, too have the Capitol citizens. Take District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close, almost unrecognizable under prosthetics and an uncanny tape facelift). She is the pinnacle of excess, from her visible cosmetic work to her neon fashion. Close is chewing so much scenery she could probably devour the entire arena, but it's exactly what the role calls for: ridiculous pomp, circumstance, and venomous hatred for the Districts.

Drusilla is one of the new characters introduced in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, a big chunk of the film's supporting cast is made up of familiar figures from the original trilogy: Capitol insider Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons); master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin); former victors Beetee, Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke); stylist Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning); and of course, President Coriolanus Snow (Ralph Fiennes). Their non-stop introductions give Sunrise on the Reaping an unfortunate case of prequel-itis, even if they play key roles in the story. Their presence also means the involvement of many new Capitol characters feels muted. Billy Porter's snake-loving stylist Magno Stift gets short shrift (and even shorter screen time), while his helpers Proserpina (Iris Apatow) and Vitus (Edvin Ryding) might as well be afterthoughts.

According to recent reports, thankfully, the District 12 newcomers fare far better. As Haymitch's great love Lenore Dove, Whitney Peak is a radiant beam of rebellious wisdom. Elsewhere, each of the tributes buck misconceptions about them to reveal their true mettle underneath. Maysilee may seem stuck-up and aloof at first, but Grace quickly unleashes the ferocious survivor in her. Wang brings kind courage to oddsmaker Wyatt, and McCann is steely sweet as Louella.

Leading it all is Zada, who does an admirable job making Haymitch his own, all while balancing Harrelson's mannerisms from the original trilogy. Put them saying "sweetheart" side by side and tell me that's not the same character, years apart.

Sunrise on the Reaping works hard to build out this captivating latest version of Panem and the Games, but once it starts really playing in that sandbox, you're in for wave after wave of brutality. It's almost impressive how, after five books and six movies, the Hunger Games franchise can still find new ways to up the emotional pain of watching children fight to death under the thumb of an authoritarian regime. You'd think we'd already hit that peak with Rue's death in the first Hunger Games, and yet!

No spoilers, but let's just say I hope Zada's contract included a bonus for each time he had to cradle the body of a dear ally and tearfully beg them to stay with him. That his performance and the film never feel stale as they go through the motions of helpless grief time and time again is a testament to how distinct each of Haymitch's relationships feel.

It has been revealed that but while Sunrise on the Reaping is arguably the Hunger Games at its most tragic, it's also the franchise at its angriest. Every instalment in the series has critiqued the Capitol, but Sunrise on the Reaping puts a laser focus on the mundane machinery that keeps these systems of power in place. As the film opens, we see Peacekeepers and Capitol staffers performing administrative tasks for the Reaping, like putting up barricades and placards dictating where children should stand. Elsewhere, the propaganda machine chugs along, with cameramen like Plutarch always finding the perfect shot to tell the Capitol's story. (And always knowing which context to leave out to make the Capitol look its absolute best.).

Throughout, though, Sunrise on the Reaping also turns its lens on Panem's citizens, asking why they allow themselves to be ruled by such a horrific regime. Collins opens Sunrise on the Reaping with several epigraphs, including two from Scottish philosopher David Hume, the first of which details his thoughts on implicit submission. The film takes that message to heart, repeatedly questioning what leads the many not to rise up against the few that govern them. Why do District 12's citizens stand mutely by while Drusilla and Plutarch re-stage a key moment from the Reaping ceremony? Why do armed tributes not turn on the unarmed Peacekeepers who oversee them at training? Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't take a subtle approach — at one point Plutarch straight-up claims "no more implicit submission" — but then again, it's also vital to see a blockbuster not sand down the novel's overt messaging.

It's also vital for a film this heavy to have hope, and almost miraculously, Sunrise on the Reaping, does. The film emphasizes the fact of its title: that for Haymitch's whole life, the sun has always risen on the Reaping. But as Lenore tells him, just because that's the way things have been for so long doesn't mean they'll be that way forever. (Their conversation remixes the novel's second epigraph from Hume.).

Anyone who's watched or read the original Hunger Games series knows that Panem will one day see a world where the sun doesn't rise on the Reaping. It'll just take a lot of work and sacrifice to get there. In Sunrise on the Reaping, we get to witness the first sparks of that eventual reunion. Knowing where Haymitch's story ends turns his tragedy into a bittersweet bridge to the future, making Sunrise on the Reaping a perfect bookend to the Hunger Games franchise as it stands. (At least, until Collins decides to return to Panem.).

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters Nov. 20.

Industry News: The Dark Side of the Moon Was the Brightest Part of 2026

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work.
  • According to recent reports, “We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew.
  • Hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts have a well-deserved reputation for being focused on their work. After spending years preparing for a single mission, they’re all business as they hurtle through the cosmos, ever vigilant that a brief lapse in concentration can mean catastrophe. That mindset is a major reason why the crew of NASA’s Artemis II was so oblivious to their celebrity as they circumnavigated the moon in April. It wasn’t until the seventh day of their nearly 10-day journey that they began to realize their exploits were causing a massive stir back home.

According to recent reports, “We were talking to our families for the second time,” recalls Jeremy Hansen, the sole Canadian in the four-person crew. “And that’s when we all heard, one after another: ‘Hey, this is really resonating on the planet in a way that you’re going to be shocked by.’”.

Hansen and his comrades were overwhelmed by their fame once they splashed back down on Earth. Nearly 150 million people had watched the mission’s key moments on NASA’s online platforms, which included feeds with near-constant access to the interior of the Orion spacecraft. The buzz around the mission harkened back to the glory days of American spaceflight, when people would gather around TV sets to marvel at astronauts floating outside their capsules or bounding around the moon.

The romantic spirit of the Artemis program’s long-term objective certainly helped: People are alive to the dream of a moon base that’s meant to serve our species’ idealistic aspirations rather than be a zillionaire’s private plaything. Artemis II supported that noble mission by putting the Orion’s life-support, navigation, and piloting systems through their paces. But fans were also drawn to the crew’s infectious energy. There was palpable chemistry between Hansen, Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman, all of whom exuded pure joy and wonder as they dealt with the minutiae of life aboard a multibillion-dollar vehicle traveling as fast as 25,000 miles per hour.

It has been revealed that “It was not a natural thing for us,” admits Hansen. “You have four type-A personalities who are willing to strap themselves to a rocket and go to the moon. We were doing stuff for the first time, and it was not uncommon for us to have four different opinions.” When the astronauts began to notice that interpersonal friction was becoming problematic during training, they enlisted the aid of professionals. During a September 2024 training trip to Iceland, the crew spent two extra days in conversations and teamwork exercises organized by Rick Rochelle, a renowned leadership guru. Once the Artemis II schedule was firmed up, the crew made a pact: Launch as friends, land as friends.

Industry observers note that their historic flight past the far side of the moon marked the apex of that friendship. They were more than 250,000 miles away from Earth. The planet looked no bigger than a fingernail sliver—“just this lifeboat hanging undisturbingly in the universe,” Koch would later say during the crew’s first public remarks after touchdown. “You look at it, and you just kind of shake your head,” notes Hansen. “How can we do anything other than lift one another up and try to make life better for one another?”.

There were plenty of lowlights during the mission, too. Some lint got trapped in the primary urine vent line, Wiseman claims, “so we had to go to a backup method of urination, which for the men wasn’t bad, but for the woman wasn’t great.” Another hiccup involved a smoke detector that erroneously went off while the spacecraft was still 80,000 miles from home, leading to 15 minutes of intense anxiety.

Sources indicate that none of the Artemis II crew members are likely to return to space: Hansen, Glover, and Wiseman have all moved on from astronaut life, and Koch transitioned into a leadership role at NASA. Their fresh, less stressful lives should give them ample opportunity to cheer on Artemis III, tentatively scheduled to launch in summer 2027—an event that may once again remind us that we’re all part of a shared story far bigger than ourselves.

#918. Latest Update: Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

Latest Update: Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.
  • Recent findings suggest that she is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator.
  • Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.

Recent findings suggest that she is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the latest Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.

Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.

Sources indicate that “My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com. “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”.

According to recent reports, rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.

In a recent development, for those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.

Industry observers note that the 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.

According to recent reports, to protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too quickly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.).

Sources indicate that the only flight-worthy tank to remain at the end of the program was ET-94. A so-called lightweight tank, it was built at a time when NASA was transitioning to a super-lightweight model and was therefore set aside. Originally slated to support a science mission on Columbia, it instead became a testbed after the tragedy, having its foam stripped off and tested to better understand what had happened.

After the program ended, NASA donated ET-94 to the California Science Center. It arrived by way of a transoceanic barge and a road trip, then sat at Exposition Park for nearly a decade.

“So much of the foam on the ET had been dissected and removed during its time as a test article that they [the California Science Center] were trying to figure out how to put it back on and blend it in to the original foam in a convincing way,” said Rosen.

There has been a longstanding debate among shuttle enthusiasts and modelers about exactly what color the external tank is, and the answer resides in the foam.

It has been revealed that “It’s orange. It’s cream. It’s burnt sienna. It just depends on the original foam, when you’re seeing it and how it’s aging. Because it starts as a kind of very ice cream-white almost color, and then depending on how long it sits out in the Sun, it turns orange,” said Rosen.

By the time she had come on staff, the decision for the most part had already been made. Dennis Jenkins, the leader of the Endeavour project, had blended a special paint called “ET Orange” that was used to cover the existing acreage “bumpy” foam. Separately, a mocha-like color was picked out for the intertank.

In a recent development, “And then the latest foam to be installed, which would have looked the newest on all of the closeout hardware—the feed lines, the ice frost ramps, the flanges around the intertank and the intertank rings—those were all the lightest color that we custom mixed. That was what we called the ice cream color,” Rosen noted.

Sources indicate that it was not only about color matching, though. For multiple reasons, the original aerospace-grade foam could not be used, so a commercial substitute had to be found that could match what Rosen described as the “orange peel.”.

It has been revealed that “If you look at the tank very closely, there’s this bumpy texture, and there is a pattern from the original manufacturing and how it was sprayed on. There’s this overlapping line, a subtle-like stripe to it,” she remarked.

Replicating that pattern was not easy.

“There was a lot of trial and error in the beginning of what we could do to try and get it to match what was already there,” Rosen told collectSPACE. “We tried taking impressions off of the real foam and making molds and casting, but that didn’t really work. I then suggested we put in a dense urethane, like plain urethane foam, and I hand-sculpt the top of it to match what was around it. That ended up becoming the best solution for fixing the acreage foam that had an orange peel-like texture.”.

Jenkins, who had worked as a space shuttle engineer and led NASA’s delivery of the orbiters to their museum homes, had high praise for Rosen and her work.

“She had to come up with a lot of fresh processes because we couldn’t apply foam the same way they did at Michoud. It’s not flightworthy by any means, but just coming up with how to make it look real took a lot of imagination on her part, and she was pretty much a one-woman show for most of it,” he stated.

According to recent reports, some of the repair work to the external tank was finished before it was lifted by crane into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center and mated with the boosters and Endeavour. From then on, Rosen had to climb scaffolding to get to her worksites.

According to recent reports, “It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on, and, I mean, I touched every inch of it,” Rosen remarked. “Once it went vertical, I was going up and down stairs. Probably the scariest was the point in the scaffolding where it just became ladders. So I had to be very, very careful and calculated in what I was doing.”.

Sources indicate that even after the scaffolding was removed in preparation for the museum opening, Rosen’s ascents were not over. A couple of weeks ago, she had to install a final component on the aft dome of the liquid hydrogen tank. To reach that, she needed a scissor lift.

Industry observers note that now that the entire Endeavour stack has made its public debut, Rosen is not parting ways with the California Science Center. Her work on ET-94 has launched her career into a new frontier.

In a recent development, “In this last year, I have been working on different artifacts with the team. I have been helping leading up to the opening. I’ve helped in ways with the different aircraft, with their assembly, their disassembly, and reassembly. I’ve done some repairs in certain areas. I’ve worked with our satellite and probe collection to do repairs and also contacted specialists outside of my realm to clean and repair thermal blankets,” said Rosen.

Industry observers note that “So I’m planning on staying with the museum for now. They’ve offered me another position, and I’m happy to stay,” she said.

The California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is now open to the public. Admission is free, but timed entry tickets are needed due to the high demand. Reservations can be made online or at 213-744-2019.

Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
  • I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
  • As recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.

I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.

As recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11. But with the cost of RAM skyrocketing this year, 8GB is once again typical for a starting configuration. The MacBook Neo got away with it, but Windows laptops, including Microsoft’s own 13-inch Surface Laptop, could struggle. Microsoft was talking a massive game about making Windows faster and more reliable before the RAM crisis really hit, and it now seems like that effort is beginning to bear fruit.

Earlier this month, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and devices, detailed in a blog post the improvements the company has made to Windows 11 to address the constraints of 8GB PCs. In it, Davuluri claims, “Windows is now up to 20% more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40% faster in our lab test.”.

In a recent development, the most significant change is in memory management. When there isn’t enough available memory to handle all active data, some of it has to be offloaded (or “paged out”) to storage. And SSDs, especially in lower-cost laptops, are much slower than RAM.

In a recent development, when Windows needs to access data that’s been paged out from the RAM to the SSD, it’s called a hard fault (or page fault). If it happens a lot — say, on a laptop with only 8GB of RAM — it leads to little slowdowns like browser tabs requiring a refresh before you can access them again. Davuluri claims, “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return.”.

It has been revealed that to test this, I fired up the same 13-inch Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM that I reviewed back in July, when I proclaimed eight is not enough for Windows. This laptop was one of the worst examples of RAMageddon’s current stranglehold on computing: With half the RAM of last year’s base model, it struggled to keep up with my regular workload. And this is Microsoft’s hardware.

Microsoft’s own laptop could struggle.

Sources indicate that before updating the Surface to the latest Windows 11 build, I got reacquainted with this laptop and the version of Windows I left it on (25H2, build 26200.8875). It was rough. Running about 20 tabs (on the latest Chrome build) while streaming a 4K YouTube video and using Slack and Signal made everything from clicking tabs to swiping around Windows with trackpad gestures feel sluggish. Chrome tabs and apps would refresh after leaving them in the background for just a short moment. When you’re multitasking and bouncing between many tabs, like when researching something, those refreshes get incredibly frustrating. And the fan was running audibly the whole time. Keeping the Resource Monitor open showed memory hard faults ranging from just under 700 faults per second to 29,000 faults per second, during which Windows ground to a halt. Seeing this number literally go off its chart showed just how badly Windows 11 struggled with memory management on 8GB before the enhancement.

It has been revealed that now, after updating the Surface Laptop to Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9974 (memory improvements are live on build 26300.9818 and beyond) things are much improved. I opened over 30 Chrome tabs while streaming the same 4K YouTube video and running the same chat apps, and Windows slowed a bit, but nowhere near as much. I could feel things like Task View get a little less responsive and at times stuttery, but it was the way you’d expect when taxing a system. Chrome tabs required less frequent refreshes. The fan also took longer to kick in and ran a little quieter and for shorter durations when it did.

Taking a fresh look at the Resource Monitor, hard faults at normal operation were now under 300 per second, with occasional jumps to about 1,000. Performance was even slightly better when I subbed out Chrome for Microsoft Edge. Edge felt more responsive under load and had fewer hard faults when running 30 tabs, the same 4K YouTube video, and a Google Meet video call.

I’m happy to see that the 8GB Surface Laptop now performs better, and I’m equally relieved that Windows 11 is starting to feel more viable on 8GB of RAM. (It’s still a shame the 8GB Surface Laptop costs more than last year’s 16GB, but I digress.) Do I want 8GB of RAM in any laptop I’m personally buying? No.

As I said when I reviewed the latest Dell XPS 13, I appreciate that 8GB is workable — and it should be fine for basic needs today — but I still advise getting 16GB if you’re able. The extra headroom will keep things speedy for longer, especially after you bog a computer down with lots of files, apps, or games. And as much better as the 8GB Surface Laptop is now, I still managed to crash Chrome entirely with fewer than three dozen tabs. Microsoft has done better by its entry-level laptop, but it’s not a miracle worker.

According to recent reports, our ongoing RAMageddon makes living with lower quantities of memory a grim reality. Microsoft is partly to blame for that, of course. And it hasn’t done itself any favors with all the feature bloat it put into Windows 11 during the Copilot / AI era. Meanwhile, other OSes, like Linux, macOS, and ChromeOS, can get by better with less. Still, I’m glad to see Microsoft ever so slightly right the ship in this one way.

The arrival of the new flagship Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max might be dominating the headlines, but the Chinese smartphone giant also just lifted the curtain on a range of accessories that are worth paying attention to.

Sources indicate that if you're a fan of open-ear audio, then the upcoming Xiaomi Clip earbuds are going to be the start of the new reveals. They're the brand's first clip-on model, and weigh just 5.5g per earbud.

If you're not familiar with this relatively recent trend, clip-on earbuds attach to your ears with a gentle clamping mechanism rather than being pushed inside your ear canal like conventional buds. This makes them highly comfortable and leaves your ear canals open to allow in background noise like traffic or conversations.

They're not a good fit for a loud commute, but such designs have become a popular choice for fitness or scenarios where you want to maintain full situational awareness while still being able to enjoy some tunes.

Xiaomi promises that the Clip earbuds will feel like they're "barely there" while in use, and accommodate a wide range of ear shapes thanks to their flexible shape-memory alloy bridge material.

In a recent development, fashion is clearly a focus, and the Xiaomi Clip earbuds are offered in four distinct colorways: Sand Gold, Pearl White, Graphite Black, and Frost Purple. They all come with a compact charging case that's designed to look something like a jewelry box.

In a recent development, as for the more technical specs, each bud contains an 11mm dynamic driver. They offer Hi-Res certified sound and support the modern LHDC 5.0 codec. According to Xiaomi, the battery life comes in at 9 hours of music playback, with an additional 29 hours offered by the charging case.

Mosseri agreed that it was the best experience for Reels on Duo, but he added that Instagram is working to make the experience on other orientations better.

In another response, Mosseri explained that Instagram was designed for tall vertical screens. The Duo's form factor is far from typical, even when folded, as it's wider and shorter compared to most smartphones. As an example of an issue Instagram is trying to address, he mentioned that it makes total sense for the navigation buttons on the right-hand side of the screen when it's closed as it's ergonomic that way. However, that's also where the Like, Comment and Share buttons are located in Reels. "Now we've got this double stack of buttons that doesn't feel great and that we need to reconsider," he said. "It's a lot of that kind of thing.".

It has been revealed that the Instagram app that was designed for the iPhone Duo has been out globally since October 23. However, it's gotten quite a bit of flak for its interface since then, with people specifically mentioning the double stack of buttons Mosseri was talking about. This could be Mosseri addressing the criticisms, or him trying to set people's expectations for when Instagram rolls out the next versions of its app for the device.

#913. Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (867 w)

Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird.
  • Discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side.
  • Industry observers note that interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird. From stormtrooper helmets to headpieces that look like they were designed for Geordi La Forge, these aren’t exactly accessories you’d want to wear in public. Which is why it was nice to unbox the Capillus HairBand and find, at long last, a normal-looking headband.

Discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side. It’s refreshing to finally see a red-light device that doesn’t embarrass the user or frighten animals and young children, but after testing it for over a month, I found the HairBand has its share of shortcomings for the price.

Industry observers note that interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap. However, the cheapest of these hats runs $1,699, and the most expensive “triple-wavelength” model, with 312 laser diodes, runs $3,299. The 2-inch-wide Capillus HairBand provides a similar laser diode treatment for less, at $599 with only 82 diodes (650 nm). (Capillus indicates the headband is designed to prioritize areas where hair loss is most noticeable, such as the hairline and temples.).

Sources indicate that unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treatment of hair follicles. I actually saw some success with this treatment when I tested the HairBand’s closest competitor, Hairmax’s LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex ($849). It couldn’t help follicles that were scarred or had already died, but studies have shown that red-light therapy can energize follicles that have more recently become dormant.

I did see some growth in the middle of my part with the LaserBand, and while I stopped using it to switch to the HairBand exclusively for the past five or so weeks, I admit this growth did make it difficult to isolate the HairBand’s contribution, especially since the headband’s coverage area is so small. Thus, the following observations are mainly on the wearing experience of the HairBand, not hair growth.

According to recent reports, at only 2 inches wide and five minutes per section, the HairBand took at least 15 minutes to cover my entire part, compared with the 3-inch-wide LaserBand, which also only needs to be used three times per week at 30 seconds per section for a total of 90 seconds. I’m a Type-A full-time working parent in my mid-forties, and let me tell you—15 minutes of doing nothing is a long time in my world.

Sources indicate that the HairBand has teeth and could sit on my head as long as it was in a normal headband position, right in the middle, but the weight of the battery pack pulls it forward ever so slightly, so if I was leaning over or doing anything that didn’t hold my head exactly straight, it would start to slip off. This meant I had to hold it with my hand, which meant no multitasking.

Capillus’ marketing materials use words like “ritual” and feature pictures of twentysomethings admiring themselves in the mirror, but I can’t imagine these women are suffering from the perimenopausal hair loss that would necessitate use of a red-light device in the first place.

I don’t consider myself to have an overly large head and have never had trouble with hats or other hair accessories, but this headband, which weighs only 6 ounces, felt quite small and somewhat precarious on my head overall. I should note it is also rather overtly feminine in style—my husband and I were able to share “custody” of the LaserBand, but he declined to wear this one, and I didn’t blame him.

There were two other concerns during my testing. One, the back of the box said it contained quick-start instructions, but my box only had the headband and USB-C charging cord—no physical user guide to be found (except online, but I had to do some googling). Not that one is needed, since it’s pretty obvious how it works—push the start button on the battery pack, and it will beep and shut off when the five minutes are up—but it’s an odd omission at this price point.

Industry observers note that two, this device is not at the moment FDA-cleared for treating hair loss or promoting regrowth. This isn’t ideal, but FDA-cleared is much different from FDA-approved; it simply requires the manufacturer to prove its product is “substantially equivalent” to an already FDA-cleared product. (And it doesn’t ensure results, just that it’s safe to use as directed.) Capillus’ rep tells me the brand is currently working on the FDA filing for the HairBand, which was released in September of this year, and intends to have it cleared in 2027. (The brand’s cap-style devices are FDA-cleared.) Even so, the HairBand is a unique device in this space, but if I’m spending that much on a red-light device, I would prefer a little more versatility in the design.

#912. Neurable One review: The brain-scanning headphones that helped me stay focused

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2200 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Neurable One review: The brain-scanning headphones that helped me stay focused

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The cans hide a wearable EEG that tracks your attention.
  • It has been revealed that I've always been fascinated by the inner workings of the human mind, and I've tested plenty of brain gadgets in my time.
  • Sources indicate that the firm describes it as a "fitness tracker for your brain," so when your attention starts to drift, the headphones will remind you to keep your focus where it needs to be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cans hide a wearable EEG that tracks your attention.

It has been revealed that I've always been fascinated by the inner workings of the human mind, and I've tested plenty of brain gadgets in my time. Sadly, all of them have been so clunky that they can only really be worn in the privacy of your own home. At least, that was the case. The Neurable One actually buries its brain-scanning technology into a pair of beefy over-ear headphones. It's designed to keep an eye on your focus levels and attention while you work, or meditate, wherever you are.

Sources indicate that the firm describes it as a "fitness tracker for your brain," so when your attention starts to drift, the headphones will remind you to keep your focus where it needs to be. And, if things continue to go wayward, you'll be advised to take a break and come back fresh rather than burning out halfway through the day. In that regard, it's been fascinating to see how the system thinks my brain operates on a regular basis.

Recent findings suggest that the Neurable One is cheaper than its predecessors and its competitors, and Neurable has improved its software platform. If there's a downside, it's that as much as I've loved my time with them, it's hard to think anyone other than nerds like me will want to use them.

Neurable spun out of a project from the University of Michigan in 2015, with the goal of building Brain Computer Interfaces (BCIs) and algorithms to interpret that data. The focus is on cognitive performance as there's plenty of military and civilian applications for the technology. Despite the name, Neurable One is actually the third pair of EEG headphones the company has made. In 2024, it partnered with Master & Dynamic on the MW75 Neuro, and a year later the Neuro LT, a lighter version of the same product addressing user comfort challenges. This time out, Neurable is going it alone without the backing of any fancy audio brands.

Industry observers note that at a glance, you'll struggle to notice much difference between this and its predecessors, as any variances are mostly aesthetic tweaks. Button placements are the same, but they're now pill-shaped rather than the circles found on the older models. The logo on the earcups has changed from M&D's icon to Neurable's signature brainwave, and there are fewer vents. In fact, the biggest difference is the loss of the cantilevered armatures joining the headband to the earcups, which have been replaced with standard hardware here.

In a recent development, it's a similar story inside the body as well; the Neurable One is more or less equipped with the same gear as before. You'll get the same 40mm Beryllium drivers, Bluetooth 5.2, AAC and aptX, albeit with six microphones — down from the eight on the MW75 Neuro. As before, each earcup has a series of dry-fit EEG sensors woven into the earpads which sit around your ear.

Neurable's pitch is to help people gain deeper insights into their own cognitive performance through the day. It contends that, much like the rest of our body, our minds have enough fuel to get us through the day, but not at full-tilt, full-pelt output. The organization indicates it's a better idea to, when your attention and focus starts to wane, take a break ahead of you burning out. Neurable argues that spending a quick five minutes staring out of the window is better than getting a headache and not functioning for an hour.

Strap the headphones on at the start of the day and the system will keep an eye on how you're doing. Do this over a period of days, or weeks, and you'll get a sense of where your focus is at its highest and lowest. You can then adjust your working patterns to suit those stats. The Neurable One works equally well when you're meditating or relaxing, giving you insights as to how and when your mind rests.

In a recent development, one of my eternal gripes with a lot of wearable EEGs (and other fabric sensors more broadly) is that the sensor pads are often fussy. They often don't work at all if they're bone dry and the skin they're in contact with is dry as well, which frustrates me. I've regularly had to gently dab the pads with cold water before running a washcloth across my forehead to dampen it. But, if the skin and pads are too wet, you'll be given a warning to dry both out, which slows you down even further. Thankfully, the Neurable One's dry-fit sensors worked from the get-go more or less every time I've used them. Every now and again, I'll be asked to push my (short) hair away from around my ears to improve the connection, but it's a world away from other products in the same field that I've tested.

According to recent reports, setup is a breeze, and the process of beginning your first session is relatively effortless, as is the daily routine you're expected to fall into. That begins with a check in at the start of the day, closing your eyes and triggering a 60-second scan of your brain. You'll get a dashboard containing your scores, with a comparison to the day before to see if things got better or worse. If you had a rough night, or if there's a lot going on, you can journal some notes on the same pane.

Industry observers note that what's far more interesting and useful are the Insights and Improve sections, which tell you both what to do to manage your cognitive load right now, and how to boost it. The former suggests that you delay major decisions, not starting jobs that need a lot of attention and grouping small, repetitive tasks together. The latter asks you to go for a quick walk in the sun, go sit in another room away from your computer for five minutes or to write down all of the things sitting in your mental cache. Once done, you can run another check-in to see if that's made any improvement.

If I'm honest, I was having a busy day at the start of a busy week, and felt snowed under by all of the projects on my desk. (In fact, my biggest issue, throughout testing these headphones, was that my Cognitive Load was always problematically high. It's almost as if working in journalism and juggling hundreds of projects all at once is somehow a problem.) The app told me that I was running low, but said I should walk up and down my stairs for a few minutes and then come back and check again. And, wouldn't you know, it actually did improve both my score and my ability to get stuff done for the rest of the morning.

According to recent reports, most days, I would set the EEG running at 9AM or so and not take them off until 12 or 1PM. The app will keep track of how well it thinks you're concentrating, letting you see that as a real time figure on screen. If it detects your focus beginning to drift, it'll rouse you back, but after a while, if you still struggle to concentrate, it'll advise you to take a short break. One thing I don't like is the way the system prods you to get back on track: When it thinks your focus is waning, you'll get a ping played in your ear as a sort of "come on, pay attention" trigger.

In a recent development, it's a harsh noise, and one that would distract me as often as it did help me drift back toward focus. You can shut off this guidance in the app, but I persevered with them even when it put me in mind of a '70s kung fu B-movie where the protagonist is asked to build a house of cards while being pelted with rotten fruit. Regularly, I'd be halfway through writing a line in what I'd describe as a flow state and then I'd get pinged, knocking me off my train of thought.

Recent findings suggest that but the more I used the headphones, the more I was able to see when the system said I was doing well and what caused slips. It became an increasingly positive feedback loop where I'd scrub through the timeline of my morning to see what I was doing when my focus was high.

As for audio quality, it's clear the company has tried to sail close to Master & Dynamic's promise of warm bass and clear treble. There's a wonderful atmosphere to the sound that makes you feel like you're in the room when it was recorded. One of my favourite tracks to test headphones with is "Finale" from the Tron: Legacy soundtrack where you can hear the horn player's breath. Wearing these, I was equally delighted to feel the rumble of the kettle drums pushing the air to my ear as they crescendoed.

The downside of Neurable no longer working with an established audio brand is that the One loses the added-value features inside the app. Whereas the previous models had a custom EQ you could fiddle with to your heart's content, here you just get the default tuning. That's not a bad thing as the audio quality here is certainly good enough, but I hope this feature can be added later. The other problem is that the app doesn't really have any sort of integration with your music app of choice, and instead will just play generic synthwave by default. Thankfully it will keep running in the background while you switch to Spotify to play actual music as you go.

Interestingly, the original MW75 Neuro weighed in at 338 grams, which was heavy enough to force the company into making a lighter version. The Neuro LT was stated to be 12 percent lighter, and you would have hoped that the Neurable One would continue that trend. Instead, it's rated for 345 grams, making it slightly heavier than the original. (In fact, the only pair of big-name cans that beats it for weight are the AirPods Max 2, which weigh in at 386.2 grams.) After a few hours of wearing the Neurable One on my head each day, I really became aware of their presence. I'll admit, I'm not an over-ears person, and so maybe those who are don't mind the sensation of having their ears pinned back for most of the day.

As for battery life, Neurable says the One will run for 22 hours, or 12 hours if you're using the EEG. When using the EEG, without ANC, I got just over 12 hours of use from the headphones before needing to head to the charger. On one hand, that's more than enough time on a charge, on the other, I'd be negligent if I didn't point out it's far below the standard for premium headphones.

In a recent development, at $499, Neurable One is a lot cheaper than the previous versions, and you get all of the insights and data on offer, without any additional paywall. There aren't many companies making consumer-grade EEG headphones, and so Neurable doesn't have much competition. The only real alternative is Brainbit which makes EEG cans for researchers, but I've asked, and it said it does sell its headphones to consumers as well. They will set you back $900, and come with a free iOS, macOS, Android or Windows app to help you monitor your mind.

According to recent reports, naturally, if you're looking for a wearable EEG that isn't built into headphones, then you also have the option of Muse. Its latest is the Muse S Athena, an EEG headband designed to help improve your meditation, but it can also monitor your brain's oxygenation levels. It'll set you back $539 with a year of Muse's premium, which adds in data about your Alpha Peak and Brain Recharge, plus it integrates with Spotify, Calm or your audiobook player of choice.

Recent findings suggest that if you'd rather just buy a pair of high-end headphones, you should instead head to Engadget's guide to the best on the market. It should go without saying that you can pick up plenty of better headphones for less — including Sony's class-leading XM6s.

I've spent a lot of time second-guessing my own recommendation, because on its own merits this is a great product. It does what it promises in an easy to use, accessible way and it's far cheaper than its (handful of) competitors. In that vacuum, it's well worth the cash, and I think I've meaningfully benefited from my time with this device. If you can afford it, and you're truly keen on learning more about how your own brain works, then I think it's worth it.

The caveat here is that it really does need to be people who are committed to doing this work on a regular basis. I suspect we're a generation or two away from a version of these cans which are truly usable by the mainstream more broadly.

Shures fresh spatial audio mic was made with creators in mind

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, spatial audio is having a moment in the creator-verse.
  • Sources indicate that "We know that more and more people — more and more creators — are kind of multidisciplinary, especially for folks who are maybe video first and then they have to worry about audio second," Steve Marek, Associate Product Manager at Shure, noted in a briefing with Mashable.
  • Marek noted, "We really wanted to think of this as a microphone that people can grow with," and that rather than having five different audio recording tools, creators can do everything with the MV360 and have flexibility with their audio output.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, spatial audio is having a moment in the creator-verse. Just last month, Sony introduced its ECM-AX10 spatial audio mic, and now Shure is entering the category with its USB-C MV360 and MV360+ spatial audio microphones.

Sources indicate that "We know that more and more people — more and more creators — are kind of multidisciplinary, especially for folks who are maybe video first and then they have to worry about audio second," Steve Marek, Associate Product Manager at Shure, noted in a briefing with Mashable. "So, we know that there's room for that industry to grow.".

Marek noted, "We really wanted to think of this as a microphone that people can grow with," and that rather than having five different audio recording tools, creators can do everything with the MV360 and have flexibility with their audio output.

Industry observers note that the MV360 retails for $349 and is available now. The microphone kit comes with the USB-C mic, a tripod, a cold shoe mic clip, a 5/8-inch mic clip, a phone clamp, two USB-C cables, a carrying case, and a foam windscreen. The microphone also has an onboard 3.5mm headphone jack.

Recent findings suggest that the MV360 features four capture modes: mono, stereo, immersive binaural, and auto tracking. The latter uses virtual microphones that steer toward the loudest sound source and is ideal for recording podcasts, interviews, or moving subjects. Regardless of capture mode, you'll get a ready-to-use two-channel audio file that requires no post-production work — though it is compatible with editing apps and devices should you want to adjust or edit.

Sources indicate that the MV360 can be as simple or as complex as you want. If you're a skilled audio engineer, you can mix to your heart's desire. Or if you've never seen audio software in your life, you have perfectly good sound straight from the mic.

According to recent reports, the MV360+ is not available yet, but will be the more advanced option geared toward field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers. It'll pair with DSLR cameras, action cameras, and 360 cameras. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Recent findings suggest that shure's MOTIV app is where you can set your capture mode and edit audio that you've recorded. There are plenty of presets and adjustable settings that you can play around with, too. Slide the level adjuster to capture every minor sound for ASMR or to avoid audio spiking. You can even select where the microphone is oriented in relation to the subject — whether it's facing up, down, or on its side. There's a little diagram in the app that highlights a sound heat map, so you can see exactly from which direction sound is hitting the microphone.

Industry observers note that you can record and edit directly in the app. And one really cool feature is that you can move "virtual microphones" after you've already recorded to better boost directional sound.

I received a test unit of the MV360 microphone ahead of its launch and have had a chance to play around with it a bit. It sounds great for unboxing videos — it picks up on all the crispy sounds without sounding blown out. I tested some whispering ASMR, and I was able to boost the audio levels in the companion app before recording to really pick up on every minor sound. I will be using this as an excuse to buy a bunch of weird candy from Five Below to further test the microphone's ASMR-ability, so stay tuned for that. We'll have a full review of the MV360 coming later.

Industry observers note that my only minor frustration with the microphone is how bulky/heavy it is. With pocket mics, like the DJI Mic Mini, there's a small receiver that you plug into your phone. The MV360 plugs directly into your phone or computer via USB-C, so it's tethered to your recording device. Clamping my phone and the mic to the tripod was just a little clunky when oriented in portrait mode. But its heft also makes sense, considering how much more advanced the audio recording is compared to small creator mics.

Also, I love that Shure includes a tripod with the MV360, but I found myself reaching for my personal tripod for most of my recordings.

Neither of those are reason enough to discredit the microphone at all — just some minor learning curves.

According to recent reports, the MV360 is available now from Shure and third-party retailers like Amazon for $349. The MV360+ will be available in early 2027 for $449.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science Corporation, the medical technology start-up founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the organization stated in a blog post.

In a recent development, investors in the fresh round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialled for fresh conditions.

Hodak unveiled that the device is now being trialled for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt’s disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

It has been revealed that with the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the US.

Recent findings suggest that still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The tech giant is at the moment designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

  • According to recent reports, he mentioned that Microsoft typically maintains two network gateway systems that connect separate systems and allow data to pass between them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was one of three root causes for the outage that affected business, hospitals, governments and other organizations worldwide.

Microsoft has revealed more details about the outage that took services like Outlook, Teams and Copilot 365 offline, affecting businesses, hospitals, law enforcement and other organizations around the world. Charles Lamanna, the company's EVP for Copilot and AI Agents, explained on X that there were three root causes for the outage.

According to recent reports, he mentioned that Microsoft typically maintains two network gateway systems that connect separate systems and allow data to pass between them. One of those gateways wasn't working for Microsoft Teams, and it overwhelmed the primary gateway. It also just so happened that nearly 14 percent of the capacity for that gateway was out of service due to an unrelated issue that happened the previous day. Those two factors caused that gateway to encounter a latent bug that's been in Microsoft's systems since July.

Industry observers note that together, the higher load that overwhelmed the gateway, the reduced server capacity and the latent bug led to a build up in traffic requests until Microsoft's servers gave out and stopped functioning. This all happened on a Thursday afternoon, during peak hours of use in the US.

Sources indicate that the outage lasted for almost a full day. Microsoft worked on fixing the concern overnight, but the bug was months-old at that point, and the company was unable to simply do a rollback in order to quickly undo the changes it had caused. In addition, its servers were overwhelmed by waiting traffic after returning to service and became unresponsive again.

In a recent development, "We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations," Lamanna wrote on his post. These details are from Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report, and the company remarked it will release more details in the final report to be released later this week.

Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds
